en: There
is one last important concept we have to
talk about, both when it comes to working
with an agent or building an agent. And
that's the concept of humans in the loop. If
you're using an AI agent and or if you're
building it for some actions, you may want
to make sure that a person has agreed to
them.
So that a model asks for a tool, makes that
tool request, but Then instead of right away
executing that tool, as we learned it thus
far,
the harness actually pauses
and asks a person for approval.
If it's in a chat, by either
asking there,
or
if it's a task-specific agent that may be
invoked via Slack, for example, by sending a
message in Slack or by sending an email and
waiting for a response
in some way. There are different ways of
implementing this technically, but the
pausing part is the relevant one here.
And then depending on whether the person
approved or refuses, the harness continues
and either executes the tool or sends a
message back to the model that the tool call
request could not be granted. And that is a
functionality that must be built into the
agent if
it is something you want.
And therefore, of course, it matters,
especially also if you're building a
task-specific agent. For example, if you are
building an agent for your company that
should handle customer refunds, you may want
to ask a human for approval there instead of
auto-approving. But it's also something you
find in many general agents that there, they
also may let you choose different approval
settings so that they also may ask you for
approval before they, for example, write a
file or run a certain command. And of
course, it's always a trade-off whether you
want a human in the loop, which slows a
model and an agent down,
but may be important for certain tools. Or
not. And the great thing, of course, is that
models as the brains of agents can work
around refusals to some extent. If a refund
was not granted by the human in the loop,
the model will only be able to work around
that refusal by drafting a message to the
customer telling them that the refund could
not be granted, for example, anything like
that. In many tools, like for example,
Claude Cowork, you can also control this, as
I mentioned. You can choose your permission
mode here, so to say.
And either automatically approve for all
critical tasks or be asked for approval.
And it then simply depends on how this agent
harness was built, what's considered a
critical task or not. But the idea of humans
in the loop is a crucial one when building
agents or when working with agents.
